# What is a UML class diagram?

The **Unified Modeling Language (UML)** is a standard way of drawing software designs. A **class diagram** shows a program's classes, what each class contains, and how the classes are related: exactly the relationships from Chapters 14 and 16.

A good class diagram lets someone write the code without asking you what you meant. That's the point of having rules.

# A note on conventions {#sec-conventions}

You'll find UML class diagrams on many websites, in textbooks and in drawing tools. The figures in these notes come from three places:

- [Visual Paradigm's UML class diagram tutorial](https://www.visual-paradigm.com/guide/uml-unified-modeling-language/uml-class-diagram-tutorial/);
- [GeeksforGeeks' article on UML class diagrams](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/system-design/unified-modeling-language-uml-class-diagrams/);
- diagrams drawn with **Mermaid**, a text-based diagram tool built into Quarto (see the source file `chap_17.qmd`).

These sources don't all draw things the same way. For example:

- GeeksforGeeks distinguishes a **directed association** (solid line, open arrow) from a plain association, and labels a dependency «use»; Visual Paradigm doesn't.
- Some figures put the class with the diamond on the left, others on the right. Either way, the diamond sits at the **whole**.
- Types may come after the name (`length : int`, the UML standard) or before it (`int length`, as in C++). Mermaid accepts both.
- Visual Paradigm writes C++-style types such as `Class6*` for a pointer; others write only the class name.
- Abstract classes and methods may be shown in *italics*, with the stereotype «abstract», or (in Mermaid) with an asterisk: `draw()*`.
- Tools colour their boxes and arrowheads differently. Colours carry no meaning.

::: {.callout-important title="The rule in this course"}
**Any convention is acceptable, in your coursework and in the exam, as long as it follows the same principles and creates no unnecessary confusion.** In practice:

1. Each class is a box: its name, then its attributes, then its operations.
2. Visibility uses `+` (public), `-` (private) and `#` (protected).
3. Relationships follow the usual line styles: solid or dashed lines; a diamond at the *whole*, filled for composition and hollow for aggregation; a hollow triangle pointing at the *parent* (or interface).
4. Multiplicities are written at the ends of a relationship.
5. **Be consistent** within one diagram, and if you use anything unusual, label it.
:::

If someone else could build the right C++ classes from your diagram without asking you a question, your diagram is good.

# Class notation

A class represents a concept that encapsulates **state** (attributes) and **behaviour** (operations). Each attribute has a type, and each operation has a **signature**. Only the class **name** is mandatory.

## Class structure

A UML class box has three compartments:

1. **the class name**, at the top;
2. **the attributes**, in the middle: these become **data members** in C++;
3. **the operations**, at the bottom: these become **member functions**.

::: {#fig-class-comparison layout-ncol=2}
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Without types or signatures"
classDiagram
    class Shape{
        -length
        +get_length()
        +set_length()
    }
```
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "With types and signatures"
classDiagram
    class Shape{
        -length: int
        +get_length() int
        +set_length(n: int) void
    }
```

The same class, drawn with less and with more detail.
:::

- **Attribute types** follow a colon: `-length : int`.
- **Return types** follow a colon at the end of the operation: `+get_length() : int`.
- **Parameter types** follow a colon after each parameter's name: `+set_length(n : int) : void`.

![A class with typed attributes and operations. Source: [Visual Paradigm](https://www.visual-paradigm.com/guide/uml-unified-modeling-language/uml-class-diagram-tutorial/).](./figures/03-class-notation-with-examples.png){width="70%"}

| | Without signatures | With full signatures |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Attribute | `-length` | `-length : int` |
| Getter | `+get_length()` | `+get_length() : int` |
| Setter | `+set_length()` | `+set_length(n : int) : void` |

## Visibility

The symbol in front of an attribute or operation gives its **visibility**, which is its access level (Chapter 11):

- `+` means **public**;
- `-` means **private**;
- `#` means **protected** (Chapter 14).

![Attributes with different visibility. Source: [Visual Paradigm](https://www.visual-paradigm.com/guide/uml-unified-modeling-language/uml-class-diagram-tutorial/).](./figures/04-class-attributes-with-different-visibility.png){width="50%"}

## Parameter direction

UML can mark each parameter as `in`, `out` or `inout`, written before the parameter's name. C++ has no such keywords; the parameter type says it instead:

| UML | Direction | Meaning | In C++ (Chapter 07) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `in` (the default) | caller to operation | the operation only reads the value | pass by value, or by `const` reference: `void f(const Fraction& x)` |
| `out` | operation to caller | the operation fills in a value for the caller | pass by non-`const` reference: `void f(int& result)` |
| `inout` | both ways | the operation reads the value, then changes it | pass by non-`const` reference: `void f(int& x)` |

![Parameter directions in a class. Source: [Visual Paradigm](https://www.visual-paradigm.com/guide/uml-unified-modeling-language/uml-class-diagram-tutorial/).](./figures/05-parameter-directionality.png){width="60%"}

## Perspectives

The same diagram can be read at different levels of detail:

- **conceptual**: the concepts in the problem domain;
- **specification**: the interfaces of the classes (what they offer);
- **implementation**: how the classes implement those interfaces.

![Perspectives of a class diagram. Source: [Visual Paradigm](https://www.visual-paradigm.com/guide/uml-unified-modeling-language/uml-class-diagram-tutorial/).](./figures/06-perspective-of-class-diagram.png)

# Relationships between classes

UML isn't just pretty pictures. Used correctly, a diagram says precisely how the code should be written, and code written from it reflects the designer's intent.

We've met all of these relationships already: inheritance (Chapter 14), realization of an interface (Chapter 15), and composition, aggregation, association and dependency (Chapter 16). Here's how two websites draw them. Notice the small differences, as discussed in @sec-conventions:

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Source: [Visual Paradigm](https://www.visual-paradigm.com/guide/uml-unified-modeling-language/uml-class-diagram-tutorial/).](./figures/07-relationships-between-classes.png)

![Source: [GeeksforGeeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/system-design/unified-modeling-language-uml-class-diagrams/).](./figures/class-diagram-relationship.png)
:::

And here they are in Mermaid:

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
direction BT
classA --|> classB : Inheritance
classC --* classD : Composition
classE --o classF : Aggregation
classG -- classH : Association
classK ..> classL : Dependency
classM ..|> classN : Realization
```

We'll go through them from the weakest to the strongest, using the classes from Chapter 16.

## Dependency ("uses a")

A **dependency** is the weakest relationship: one class *uses* another for a moment, as a parameter or a local variable, without keeping it. If the class it uses changes, it may have to change too.

- **Logic:** "class A uses class B to do a task."
- **Notation:** a **dashed** line with an open arrow, pointing at the class being used.
- **Example (Chapter 16):** `Point` uses `std::ostream` in its `operator<<`. Likewise, a `Printer` uses a `Document` to print, but doesn't own it.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Point
    class ostream
    Point ..> ostream : uses
```

## Association ("knows a")

An **association** is a structural link between two otherwise unrelated classes. It can be **unidirectional** (one class knows about the other) or **bidirectional** (both know about each other).

- **Logic:** "class A is associated with class B."
- **Notation:** a **solid** line. With an open arrowhead, it's a *directed* association: only the class at the tail knows about the other. With no arrowhead, it's bidirectional.
- **Example (Chapter 16):** a `Doctor` and a `Patient`. They know about each other, but neither owns the other.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Doctor
    class Patient
    Doctor "0..*" -- "0..*" Patient : treats
```

## Aggregation ("has a")

An **aggregation** is a whole–part relationship in which the parts can exist independently of the whole.

- **Logic:** "class A has a class B, but B can live without A."
- **Notation:** a solid line with a **hollow diamond** at the **whole**.
- **Example (Chapter 16):** a `Department` and its `Teacher`s. Closing the department doesn't destroy the teachers. Likewise a `Library` and its `Book`s.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Department
    class Teacher
    Department o-- Teacher
```

## Composition ("part of")

A **composition** is a strong whole–part relationship: the whole manages the part's lifetime. Destroy the whole, and the parts go with it.

- **Logic:** "class B is an integral part of class A."
- **Notation:** a solid line with a **filled diamond** at the **whole**.
- **Example (Chapter 16):** a `Creature` and its `Point2D` location. Likewise a `House` and its `Room`s: demolish the house, and the rooms are gone.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Creature
    class Point2D
    Creature *-- Point2D : location
```

## Inheritance, or generalization ("is a")

**Inheritance** means a derived (child) class inherits the attributes and operations of its base (parent) class: it's a specialized version of a more general concept.

- **Logic:** "class B is a kind of class A."
- **Notation:** a solid line with a **hollow triangle** pointing at the **parent**.
- **Example (Chapter 14):** a `Lecturer` is a `UniPerson`, and so is a `Student`.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction BT
    class UniPerson
    class Lecturer
    class Student
    UniPerson <|-- Lecturer
    UniPerson <|-- Student
```

## Realization ("implements")

**Realization** connects an **interface** to a class that implements it. The class *realizes* the contract that the interface defines. In C++, an interface is an abstract class with only pure virtual functions (Chapter 15).

- **Logic:** "class A implements everything interface B promises."
- **Notation:** a **dashed** line with a **hollow triangle** pointing at the interface.
- **Example (Chapter 15):** `Circle` and `Rectangle` implement the `Shape` interface.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction BT
    class Shape {
        <<interface>>
        +area() double
        +name() string_view
    }
    class Circle
    class Rectangle
    Shape <|.. Circle
    Shape <|.. Rectangle
```

::: {.callout-note title="Realization or inheritance?"}
Strictly, realization is for **interfaces**. A class derived from an abstract class that *also* has data or implemented functions (like Chapter 15's `Animal`) is drawn with ordinary inheritance: a solid line. Many websites and tools blur this distinction. Following @sec-conventions, either is accepted, as long as you're consistent.
:::

## Abstract classes

An abstract class can't be instantiated (Chapter 15), and the diagram should make that visible. There are two common ways:

- **italics**: the class name in *italics*, and each abstract (pure virtual) operation in *italics* too;
- **a stereotype**: the word «abstract» above the class name. It's clearer in hand-drawn diagrams, where italics are hard to see.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction BT
    class Animal {
        <<abstract>>
        #name: string
        +get_name() string_view
        +speak()* string_view
    }
    class Cow {
        +speak() string_view
    }
    Animal <|-- Cow
```

In Mermaid, `speak()*` marks an abstract operation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Abstract classes in the paper exam"}
Handwriting has no italics, so use either of these:

- write «abstract» (or `<<abstract>>`) above the class name;
- surround the name with asterisks, `*ClassName*`, as if it were italic (Markdown style).
:::

## Summary of relationships

| Relationship | In words | Lifetime | Notation |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Dependency | "uses a" (for a moment) | independent | dashed line, open arrow (- - >) |
| Association | "knows a" | independent | solid line (──), with an open arrow if directed |
| Aggregation | "has a" | independent | solid line, hollow diamond at the whole (◇──) |
| Composition | "part of" | the whole manages the part | solid line, filled diamond at the whole (◆──) |
| Inheritance | "is a" | the derived object contains the base part | solid line, hollow triangle at the parent (──▷) |
| Realization | "implements" | (a contract) | dashed line, hollow triangle at the interface (- - ▷) |

# Multiplicity

**Multiplicity** (often called **cardinality**) says how many objects of one class can be linked to one object of the other. It's written at the ends of a relationship.

| Notation | Meaning | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `0..1` | zero or one | an `Employee` may have a `Desk` |
| `1` | exactly one | a `Car` has exactly one `Engine` |
| `0..*` | zero or more | a `Folder` contains any number of `File`s |
| `1..*` | one or more | a `Team` has at least one `Player` |
| `*` | many | short for `0..*` |
| `n` | exactly n | a `Tricycle` has exactly `3` `Wheel`s |
| `m..n` | between m and n | a `Jury` has between `6` and `12` members |

## Multiplicity examples

As discussed in @sec-conventions, it's fine to write an attribute's type before its name, as below, or after it.

**Example 1.** A `Car` has four `Tire`s and one `Engine`: compositions with fixed multiplicities.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Car {
        +String model
        +start_engine()
    }
    class Tire {
        +int pressure
    }
    class Engine {
        +int horse_power
    }
    Car "1" *-- "4" Tire : has
    Car "1" *-- "1" Engine : has
```

**Example 2.** A `Library` holds any number of `Book`s and `CD`s: aggregations with "many".

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction BT
    class Library {
        +String branch_name
        +open()
    }
    class Book {
        +String isbn
        +String title
    }
    class CD {
        +String artist
        +int track_count
    }
    Library "1" o-- "0..*" Book : contains
    Library "1" o-- "0..*" CD : contains
```

**Example 3.** A `Doctor` treats many `Patient`s, and a `Patient` may see many `Doctor`s: a many-to-many association.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Doctor {
        +String name
        +String specialization
        +schedule_appointment()
    }
    class Patient {
        +String name
        +Date date_of_birth
        +view_medical_history()
    }
    Doctor "0..*" -- "0..*" Patient : treats
```

# Larger examples

## Flights, pilots and airports

`Flight`, `Pilot` and `Airport` are linked by **associations**:

- a `Pilot` *works* a `Flight`: a relationship of service, not a structural "part of";
- an `Airport` hosts many `Flight`s, and each `Flight` departs from one `Airport` and arrives at another.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    class Flight {
        -String flight_number
        -DateTime departure_time
        +delay_flight(int minutes)
    }
    class Pilot {
        -String license_number
        +String name
        +get_flight_hours() double
    }
    class Airport {
        -String iata_code
        +String city
        +get_weather() String
    }
    Flight "0..*" -- "2" Pilot : flown by
    Flight "0..*" -- "1" Airport : departs from
    Flight "0..*" -- "1" Airport : arrives at
```

## Departments, lecturers, students and courses

1. A `Department` has many `Lecturer`s.
2. A `Department` has many `Student`s.
3. A `Department` offers many `Course`s.
4. Several `Lecturer`s can teach one `Course`.
5. One `Lecturer` can teach several `Course`s.
6. One `Student` can take many `Course`s.
7. One `Course` can have many `Student`s.

Statements 1 to 3 describe "part of the department": aggregations, since lecturers, students and courses don't disappear if the department is reorganized. Statements 4 to 7 describe *providing* and *using* a service: associations.

::: {.callout-note}
In everyday English we could say "has" for every one of these sentences. But a student rarely moves between departments during their studies, while lecturers change courses quite often. The lecturer–course and student–course links are interactions that come and go, which is what associations describe.
:::

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    class Department {
        -String name
        +add_lecturer(Lecturer l)
        +add_course(Course c)
    }
    class Lecturer {
        -String staff_id
        +String name
        +get_specialization() String
    }
    class Student {
        -String student_id
        +double gpa
    }
    class Course {
        -String course_id
        -int credits
    }
    Department "1" o-- "1..*" Lecturer : employs
    Department "1" o-- "1..*" Student : manages
    Department "1" o-- "1..*" Course : offers
    Lecturer "1..*" -- "1..*" Course : teaches
    Student "1..*" -- "1..*" Course : enrolled in
```

# From the diagram to C++

This is what the exam asks of you: read a diagram, and write the classes, or the other way round. The usual translations:

| In the diagram | In C++ |
|:---|:---|
| class box | `class Name { ... };` |
| attribute `-x : double` | private data member `double x{};` |
| operation `+f(n : int) : void` | public member function `void f(int n);` |
| composition, multiplicity `1` | an ordinary data member: `Point2D location{};` |
| composition, multiplicity `*` | a `std::vector` of members, or `std::unique_ptr`s the class owns |
| aggregation | a reference or pointer to an outside object; for many, `std::vector<std::reference_wrapper<T>>` |
| association | pointer members (for many, `std::vector<const T*>`), on one or both sides |
| dependency | a function parameter or a local variable, not a member |
| inheritance | `class Derived : public Base` |
| realization | inherit from an interface and override every pure virtual function |
| abstract operation | a pure virtual function: `virtual double area() const = 0;` |

# Past paper exam: shapes

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    class Shape {
        <<abstract>>
        +draw()* void
    }
    class Point {
        +float x
        +float y
    }
    class Polygon {
        +draw() void
    }
    class Rectangle {
        -float width
        -float height
        -float theta
        +draw() void
    }
    class Square
    class Ellipse {
        -float width
        -float height
        -float theta
        +draw() void
    }
    class Circle

    Shape <|.. Polygon
    Shape <|.. Ellipse
    Polygon <|-- Rectangle
    Rectangle <|-- Square
    Ellipse <|-- Circle

    Polygon "1" *-- "3..*" Point : vertices
    Rectangle "1" *-- "1" Point : bottom-left corner
    Ellipse "1" *-- "1" Point : centre
```

- `Polygon` and `Ellipse` must list `+draw() : void`: they implement the abstract operation of `Shape`.
- Repeating `+draw() : void` in `Square` and `Circle` is allowed, but unnecessary: they inherit it.
- `Shape` is abstract, with an abstract `draw()`. The dashed realization arrows from `Polygon` and `Ellipse` follow the "implements" reading of @sec-conventions. Solid inheritance arrows would be accepted too.
